metadata.notes: Paraphrased synthesis from official coaching/rules resources and peer-reviewed biomechanics, sports medicine, and physical-demand literature. No database records have been created.
metadata.research_goal: Create backend-ready tennis stroke mechanics and racket-skill knowledge covering grips, ready position, forehand, backhand, slice, serve, return, volley, overhead, contact point, spin, kinetic chain, common errors, level teaching progressions, stroke-specific physical demands, load risks, and backend records.

key_concepts.concept: Grip, contact zone, and spin are linked variables.
key_concepts.summary: Continental grips support serves, volleys, overheads, and slice because the racket face can be managed with a stable wrist. Eastern through western forehand grips progressively make higher and more forward topspin contact easier, but can make low balls and grip changes harder.
key_concepts.coaching_use: Teach grips through the ball flight and contact shape they create, not as isolated hand labels.

key_concepts.concept: Ready position is a live transition state.
key_concepts.summary: The athlete should land or settle from the split step with athletic posture, racket in front, eyes reading the opponent, and enough balance to move in any direction.
key_concepts.coaching_use: Assess whether the player is ready before the opponent contacts the ball and whether first-step quality improves after the split step.

key_concepts.concept: Early unit turn organizes the stroke before the arm accelerates.
key_concepts.summary: Forehands, backhands, volleys, returns, and overheads all benefit from early shoulder-trunk preparation so the arm is not responsible for all racket speed or face control.
key_concepts.coaching_use: Use opponent contact as the cue for split step and ball recognition as the cue for unit turn.

key_concepts.concept: There is no single perfect contact point.
key_concepts.summary: Contact depends on stroke, grip, stance, ball height, incoming speed and spin, intended trajectory, and time pressure. Serves and overheads need high contact; volleys need compact contact in front; groundstrokes vary by grip and ball height.
key_concepts.coaching_use: Store contact zones by stroke and ball context rather than one global cue.

key_concepts.concept: Technique should be tied to ball controls.
key_concepts.summary: Tennis technique becomes useful when it reliably controls height, depth, direction, speed, and spin under changing ball conditions.
key_concepts.coaching_use: Backend skill records should include ball-control outcomes, not only visual body positions.

key_concepts.concept: Spin is a product of racket path, racket face, contact friction, and speed.
key_concepts.summary: Topspin usually needs an upward and forward brushing component with enough racket speed; slice needs a more downward-to-forward or high-to-low component with face stability; flat drives reduce vertical brushing while keeping depth control.
key_concepts.coaching_use: Progress spin by asking for ball flight and bounce outcomes before refining small hand details.

key_concepts.concept: Efficient strokes use a coordinated kinetic chain.
key_concepts.summary: Legs, hips, trunk, shoulder, arm, wrist, and racket should transfer energy in a timed sequence. Breaks in the chain often show up as arm-dominant strokes, late contact, poor balance, or excess joint stress.
key_concepts.coaching_use: Flag arm-only solutions as both performance and load issues.

key_concepts.concept: Open, semi-open, neutral, and closed stances are contextual choices.
key_concepts.summary: Open and semi-open stances help manage wide or fast balls and rotational recovery; neutral or more closed stances can support forward transfer, lower balls, approach shots, and one-handed backhands.
key_concepts.coaching_use: Do not mark one stance as universally correct; record preferred stance by stroke and tactical situation.

key_concepts.concept: Follow-through and deceleration protect accuracy and tissue.
key_concepts.summary: Good strokes accelerate through contact and then dissipate force through the trunk, shoulder, arm, and lower body. Abrupt braking or cramped follow-through can degrade control and increase load.
key_concepts.coaching_use: Assess the finish as evidence of balance, timing, and load distribution.

key_concepts.concept: Serve mechanics need separate backend modeling.
key_concepts.summary: The serve includes stance, toss, loading, cocking, acceleration, contact, follow-through, landing, and recovery. It has high shoulder, elbow, trunk, and lower-limb load compared with most cooperative rally work.
key_concepts.coaching_use: Track serve count and high-intent serve count separately from total hitting volume.

key_concepts.concept: Return of serve is not just a normal groundstroke.
key_concepts.summary: The return uses earlier reading, split-step timing, compact preparation, strong contact stability, and tactical choices based on first or second serve pressure.
key_concepts.coaching_use: Record return as a separate skill with reaction, contact, and tactical constraints.

key_concepts.concept: Volley technique prioritizes racket-face control and body movement over a large swing.
key_concepts.summary: The volley is usually prepared with a continental grip, short shoulder turn, stable wrist, contact in front, and movement through the ball when time allows.
key_concepts.coaching_use: Teach volley as interception and placement before adding pace.

key_concepts.concept: The overhead combines ball tracking, movement, and serve-like striking.
key_concepts.summary: The player must move under a descending ball, create a high contact point, and recover balance after contact. Many errors come from poor tracking or late preparation rather than racket mechanics alone.
key_concepts.coaching_use: Assess footwork and spacing before changing the arm action.

key_concepts.concept: Slice is both a defensive control stroke and an attacking disruption stroke.
key_concepts.summary: Backhand slice can neutralize pace, keep the ball low, change rhythm, approach the net, or force an opponent to hit up.
key_concepts.coaching_use: Store slice as a separate tactical tool, not only as a weaker backhand variation.

key_concepts.concept: Drop shots, lobs, and approach shots depend heavily on court context.
key_concepts.summary: These strokes require disguise, opponent-position reading, contact feel, and recovery planning. Poor choices often fail even when the stroke execution is technically clean.
key_concepts.coaching_use: Backend records should tie these shots to opponent depth, player position, and next-ball responsibility.

key_concepts.concept: Beginner technique should be scaled to create rally success.
key_concepts.summary: Reduced court size, lower-compression balls, simpler grips, shorter swings, and cooperative rally tasks improve learning without forcing adult-sized timing demands too early.
key_concepts.coaching_use: Use Play and Stay style constraints before heavy technical correction.

key_concepts.concept: Intermediate players need technical skills under realistic pressure.
key_concepts.summary: Once basic contact is stable, drills should add movement, recovery, target decisions, serve-return constraints, and scoring pressure.
key_concepts.coaching_use: Promote from cooperative repetition to constrained live-ball tasks.

key_concepts.concept: Advanced stroke skill is adaptable rather than visually identical.
key_concepts.summary: Higher-level players vary height, spin, direction, tempo, contact timing, and stance to solve different tactical problems while preserving repeatable contact quality.
key_concepts.coaching_use: Advanced assessments should score ball outcome and decision quality, not cosmetic technique alone.

key_concepts.concept: Common errors should be corrected by root cause.
key_concepts.summary: Late contact may come from poor ready timing, slow unit turn, wrong spacing, grip-contact mismatch, or overlarge swing. Correcting only the visible miss can create compensations.
key_concepts.coaching_use: Error records should include likely causes, observable signs, and first intervention.

key_concepts.concept: Technique and load management should be connected.
key_concepts.summary: High-volume serving, heavy topspin forehands, one-handed backhands, overheads, and firm volleys stress different tissues. Skill plans should adapt to pain response, recent volume, and upcoming match density.
key_concepts.coaching_use: Add load flags and pain gates to stroke records before app-facing program generation.

model.backend_use: Attach errors to observable signs, likely causes, and first coaching intervention instead of storing generic corrections.

common_errors: attack shot selected from defensive court position

level_progressions.beginner: Correct one root cause at a time and preserve rally success.
level_progressions.intermediate: Use outcome constraints to expose errors under movement and decision pressure.
level_progressions.advanced: Use video, match charting, and load response to separate technical issue from tactical or fatigue issue.

tactical_rules.rule: Use crosscourt as the default rally pattern when neutral.
tactical_rules.rationale: Crosscourt gives more court length and net margin, supports recovery, and reduces unnecessary change-of-direction risk.

tactical_rules.rule: Change direction down the line mainly from balanced contact, attackable ball height, or clear tactical need.
tactical_rules.rationale: Down-the-line redirection has less net and court margin and often exposes recovery if the shot is not assertive.

tactical_rules.rule: Establish depth before chasing angle for most developing players.
tactical_rules.rationale: Depth pushes the opponent back and protects against short replies; sharp angle requires better contact and recovery awareness.

tactical_rules.rule: Use height and topspin to reset when stretched or defending.
tactical_rules.rationale: A higher, deeper ball buys recovery time and reduces low-percentage counterattack decisions.

tactical_rules.rule: Serve location should anticipate the plus-one ball.
tactical_rules.rationale: Serve effectiveness is not only ace rate; it includes the predictable return location and the next stroke opportunity.

tactical_rules.rule: Second serves should prioritize spin, height, and placement margin before speed.
tactical_rules.rationale: Double-fault risk and point-start pressure make controllable spin and location more valuable than unsupported pace.

tactical_rules.rule: Treat first-serve returns and second-serve returns as different tactical tasks.
tactical_rules.rationale: First serves often require compact blocking and depth; second serves can be attacked with earlier positioning, direction choice, or heavier spin.

tactical_rules.rule: Low volleys usually need depth and control; high volleys can be directed more aggressively.
tactical_rules.rationale: Low contact reduces attacking options and increases net risk; high contact allows more downward or angled finishing.

tactical_rules.rule: Approach only with a coverage plan for pass, lob, and first volley.
tactical_rules.rationale: Approach quality includes the hit, net position, split-step timing, and likely opponent reply.

tactical_rules.rule: Use slice to lower contact height and disrupt rhythm rather than only to survive.
tactical_rules.rationale: A well-placed slice can force the opponent to hit up, move forward, or generate pace without a comfortable strike zone.

tactical_rules.rule: Use drop shots mainly from balanced, inside-court, or opponent-deep contexts.
tactical_rules.rationale: Drop shots from defensive positions often become short, readable, or punishable balls.

tactical_rules.rule: Use lob when the net player closes too far, leans forward, or when the hitter needs recovery time.
tactical_rules.rationale: The lob changes the vertical problem, can beat aggressive net positioning, and can reset defensive court position.

tactical_rules.rule: Earlier contact can take time away only when balance and spacing are good.
tactical_rules.rationale: On-the-rise and early contact are attacking tools, but late preparation turns them into error sources.

tactical_rules.rule: Choose spin based on score pressure and risk tolerance.
tactical_rules.rationale: Higher net clearance and heavier spin can lower error risk on pressure points, while flatter speed is more appropriate from clear attack positions.

tactical_rules.rule: Attack the short ball, but do not assume every inside-court ball is attackable.
tactical_rules.rationale: Ball height, spin, body balance, and opponent position determine whether the player should drive, slice, drop, or reset.

physical_demands.demand: Serve and overhead require coordinated leg drive, trunk rotation/extension control, scapular control, shoulder rotation, forearm contribution, and landing recovery.
physical_demands.planning_note: High-intent serve or overhead sessions should account for shoulder, elbow, trunk, and lower-limb fatigue.

physical_demands.demand: Forehand production relies on repeated lower-body loading, trunk rotation, shoulder-arm acceleration, and deceleration after high racket speed.
physical_demands.planning_note: Heavy forehand blocks need trunk, hip, shoulder, forearm, and wrist capacity support.

physical_demands.demand: One-handed backhand places high demands on early preparation, shoulder control, forearm endurance, wrist stability, and spacing precision.
physical_demands.planning_note: Progress high-volume or high-ball one-hander work gradually, especially after elbow or shoulder symptoms.

physical_demands.demand: Two-handed backhand uses trunk rotation and bilateral arm contribution, with the non-dominant side often providing meaningful drive and control.
physical_demands.planning_note: Train non-dominant shoulder, forearm, and trunk strength rather than assuming the dominant arm does all work.

physical_demands.demand: Slice requires stable racket-face control, shoulder-led path, forearm/wrist stability, and lower-body flexion for low contacts.
physical_demands.planning_note: Repeated low slice drills add trunk and hip hinge demand along with forearm control demand.

physical_demands.demand: Return of serve requires rapid perception, split-step timing, short-distance acceleration, trunk bracing, compact swing speed, and impact stability.
physical_demands.planning_note: Return training should include reaction and ball-speed exposure, not only stationary feeds.

physical_demands.demand: Volleying requires repeated split steps, lunges, short accelerations, stable hand-racket position, and quick recovery for the next ball.
physical_demands.planning_note: Net sessions can create calf, groin, knee, and forearm fatigue even without long groundstroke rallies.

physical_demands.demand: Drop shots and lobs require fine racket control, visual tracking, balance, and rapid transition after contact.
physical_demands.planning_note: Treat touch work as skill-dense; it can be lower metabolic load but still cognitively and coordinatively demanding.

physical_demands.demand: Approach play combines forward acceleration, controlled contact while moving, braking into net position, and split-step timing before the opponent hits.
physical_demands.planning_note: Approach drills stress deceleration and lower-limb control more than stationary hitting blocks.

physical_demands.demand: Heavy spin production needs racket-head speed plus repeated forearm, wrist, shoulder, and trunk control.
physical_demands.planning_note: Heavy topspin blocks should be counted differently from easy cooperative rally volume.

physical_demands.demand: Most match contacts occur after acceleration, braking, or adjustment steps, requiring dynamic balance rather than stationary form.
physical_demands.planning_note: Progress from stationary to movement-fed contact before declaring a stroke match-ready.

physical_demands.demand: Tennis demands repeated high-intensity bursts with incomplete recovery across rallies, games, sets, and tournament days.
physical_demands.planning_note: Conditioning should preserve stroke quality under repeated effort rather than use generic fatigue only.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: High-intent serve volume can overload shoulder, elbow, trunk, and lower limb tissues.
risk_signals: shoulder or elbow soreness during acceleration
injury_or_load_risks.load_management: Track serve count, high-intent count, second-serve spin count, and next-day shoulder/elbow/back response.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Arm-dominant serving increases stress when leg drive and trunk sequencing are poor.
risk_signals: serve speed generated by shoulder effort only
injury_or_load_risks.load_management: Reduce high-intent serves while rebuilding throw-like sequencing and landing mechanics.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Late forehand contact can shift load to wrist, elbow, and shoulder while reducing accuracy.
injury_or_load_risks.load_management: Address ready timing, unit turn, spacing, and swing size before adding volume.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Heavy topspin volume can accumulate forearm, wrist, shoulder, and trunk load.
risk_signals: loss of depth despite high spin
injury_or_load_risks.load_management: Separate heavy-spin blocks from easy rally volume and avoid sudden jumps in spin-intent work.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: One-handed backhand errors can increase elbow, forearm, wrist, and shoulder load.
injury_or_load_risks.load_management: Use lower-speed feeds, reduce high-ball volume, and build shoulder/forearm capacity before intense one-hander blocks.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Two-handed backhand contact too close to the body can provoke wrist, elbow, shoulder, or trunk compensation.
injury_or_load_risks.load_management: Use spacing drills and compact preparation before increasing pace or return speed.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Chopping or wrist-carving slice can overload wrist and elbow while producing poor depth.
risk_signals: ball floats or dies into net
injury_or_load_risks.load_management: Train shoulder-led forward path, knee flexion for low balls, and reduced carving volume.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Firm-grip reaction volleys and mishits can load wrist, elbow, and shoulder, especially at high ball speed.
injury_or_load_risks.load_management: Progress ball speed and reaction distance gradually while preserving face stability and body movement.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Overhead repetition adds serve-like shoulder and trunk load plus tracking and backward movement risk.
injury_or_load_risks.load_management: Count overheads with serve/overhead load, teach turn-and-track, and avoid fatigued high-volume smash blocks.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Repeated drop-shot attempts from poor balance can stress wrist/forearm and reinforce avoidant stroke mechanics.
risk_signals: frequent short-ball errors from behind baseline
injury_or_load_risks.load_management: Gate drop-shot work by balance, court position, and pain-free touch control.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Approach and net-transition drills increase braking, lunge, calf, groin, knee, and ankle load.
risk_signals: calf or Achilles tightness after forward drills
injury_or_load_risks.load_management: Progress forward approach volume with lower-limb deceleration capacity and surface considerations.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Fatigue can reduce spacing, split-step timing, trunk control, and contact quality across strokes.
risk_signals: late contact increases late in session
balance errors and rushed decisions increase
injury_or_load_risks.load_management: Use session RPE, duration, stroke counts, and quality drop-off as progression gates.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: New grips, swing paths, serve mechanics, or racket/string changes can shift tissue load quickly.
risk_signals: new soreness after equipment or grip change

injury_or_load_risks.load_management: Treat technical changes as load changes and introduce them in low-volume, low-stakes blocks first.

training_implications.implication: Beginner sessions should prioritize rally success, simple grips, stable contact, and cooperative constraints before complex technique.
training_implications.backend_rule: Do not assign high-volume serve or advanced pattern work until basic contact and pain-free rally tolerance are present.

training_implications.implication: Scaled courts, lower-compression balls, and shorter target distances are legitimate technical tools, not only youth modifications.
training_implications.backend_rule: Allow technical progressions to reduce ball speed and bounce height before increasing court size or pace.

training_implications.implication: Every stroke drill should define the intended ball-control outcome.
training_implications.backend_rule: Require target fields for height, depth, direction, speed, or spin in app-facing stroke drills.

training_implications.implication: Grip changes should be trained inside ready-position and recovery drills rather than only during static instruction.
training_implications.backend_rule: Add grip-change assessment to serve-return, approach-volley, and slice-to-drive progressions.

training_implications.implication: Serve development needs quality gates and volume caps.
training_implications.backend_rule: Increase high-intent serve count only when toss, contact, landing, and next-day symptom response are acceptable.

training_implications.implication: Return training should be programmed separately from baseline groundstroke training.
training_implications.backend_rule: Include compact preparation, split-step timing, first-serve block, and second-serve attack variants in return records.

training_implications.implication: Forehand development should move from cooperative contact to crosscourt depth, then movement, then tactical variation.
training_implications.backend_rule: Gate advanced forehand options by contact quality, depth control, and recovery after wide balls.

training_implications.implication: One-handed and two-handed backhands need distinct progressions and load flags.
training_implications.backend_rule: Store backhand type as a player attribute that changes contact, progression, tactical options, and risk flags.

training_implications.implication: Slice should be taught as a required tactical skill even for players with strong two-handed backhands.
training_implications.backend_rule: Create slice records for neutralization, approach, short-ball touch, and return variation.

training_implications.implication: Volley training should include approach, split step, first volley, recovery, and overhead response.
training_implications.backend_rule: Do not store volleys only as static net feeds; include transition context.

training_implications.implication: Overhead instruction should start with recognition, turn, movement, and spacing before power.
training_implications.backend_rule: Require overhead assessment to include tracking and position under the ball, not just contact result.

training_implications.implication: Drop, lob, and approach shots should be constrained by opponent position, court position, and balance.
training_implications.backend_rule: Skill records should include decision cues and recovery tasks, not only execution cues.

training_implications.implication: S&C for stroke mechanics should support rotational power, trunk control, scapular function, forearm capacity, and lower-limb braking.
training_implications.backend_rule: Map stroke blocks to physical qualities: rotation, deceleration, shoulder/scapular endurance, forearm/wrist capacity, and aerobic recovery.

training_implications.implication: Technical sessions should stop or reduce intensity when quality drop-off changes mechanics or pain response.
training_implications.backend_rule: Use quality signals such as late contact, toss breakdown, loss of depth, or pain as stop rules.

training_implications.implication: Advanced players need variable practice under score, target, opponent, and fatigue constraints.
training_implications.backend_rule: Progress advanced technical records into tactical scenarios such as serve-plus-one, return-plus-one, break point, and short-ball conversion.
